title: Just Staying in Touch?
gist: Social media is often defended as 'phatic' communication where keeping in touch matters more than content, but the author argues the Malinowski concept translates poorly: fragmented, multi-channel attention and Bauman-style liquid connections yield enormous phatic volume without the durable bonds phatic talk was meant to build.

themes.theme: Messaging volume explosion vs. content vacuity

insights.claim: Pew Research Center reported in 2012 that the average 18-24-year-old American smartphone user sent 60 text messages per day, up from 50 in 2009, a figure that now looks low.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Baseline for how fast messaging intensity has grown among young users; useful context for engagement-driven platform models.
insights.quote: sent sixty text messages per day, up from the fifty the same demographic cohort dispatched daily in 2009

insights.claim: Facebook reported that its WhatsApp and Messenger apps handle more than sixty billion messages per day, on top of roughly half a million posts made each minute on Facebook itself.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Scale of Meta's messaging graph underlines that its moat is connection volume, not content quality.
insights.quote: its WhatsApp and Messenger apps field more than sixty billion messages per day

insights.claim: Critiques of social media's trivial content miss the point, because on these platforms keeping in touch, not content, is what users are actually consuming.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Platform value should be judged on connection-maintenance metrics (frequency, reach) rather than content substance.
insights.quote: “content is not king” in this domain; “‘keeping in touch’ is.”
insights.locator: But perhaps, as some observers have countered

themes.theme: From Malinowski's phatic communion to Jakobson's phatic function

insights.claim: Anthropologist Bronislaw Malinowski framed 'phatic communion' as small talk whose meaning is sociability itself, a universal human desire for the mere presence of others, but his examples assumed face-to-face encounters and ignored the telephone and telegraph.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Explains why low-information chatter is a durable demand driver for communication products across eras.
insights.quote: ties of union are created by a mere exchange of words
insights.locator: But Malinowski also perceived that something

insights.claim: Roman Jakobson's 1956 phatic function relocated small talk to telecommunications, where its job is to check that the channel works and to hold the attention of a listener who might drift away.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Much of modern app design (read receipts, typing indicators, pings) is phatic channel-checking that keeps users on the line.
insights.quote: to check whether the channel works (“Hello, do you hear me?”)

insights.claim: Researchers now treat emojis, likes, favorites, upvotes and even breakfast snapshots as a phatic symbology specific to new media, where meaning lies in the connection rather than the content.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Engagement signals like likes function as relationship maintenance, which is why they sustain usage despite low informational value.
insights.quote: The meaning lies in the connection, not the content.

insights.claim: Unlike speech, visual social-media interfaces let users run several conversations at once across platforms and speeds, so both sides of an exchange routinely split attention across multiple open channels.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Fragmented attention is a structural feature of the medium; platforms compete for slices of parallel attention rather than whole sessions.
insights.quote: The flickering of attention is, we might say, now a built-in feature.
insights.locator: Perhaps we can say that Jakobson

insights.claim: As networks keep growing, users compress phatic communication into deferred, asynchronous, non-intrusive deposits, effectively eliminating extended back-and-forth dialogue; many people now have time only for a few clicks.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Network size growth trades off against depth of interaction, pointing to demand for lower-effort engagement formats.
insights.quote: The problem is that many of us now have time only for those few clicks.

themes.theme: Liquid modernity: phatic talk without communion

insights.claim: Social media produces unprecedented volumes of phatic communication but often without the durable bonds Malinowski saw as its purpose, so phatic messages frequently lead only to more phatic messages.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Points to a loneliness and connection-quality gap that platforms monetize but do not fill, a recurring source of regulatory and reputational risk.
insights.quote: Phatic communication now often functions—or is it dysfunctions?—as a prelude merely to more phatic communication.
insights.locator: So much of what we do on social media

insights.claim: Sociologist Zygmunt Bauman called the Internet a 'realm and nursery of phatic expressions' that discourages anything weightier, singling out Twitter as the worst offender, and saw social media as offering reassuring contact that can be dropped easily.
insights.speaker: Richard Hughes Gibson
insights.so_what: Low-commitment connection is the product; the critique flags Twitter-style formats as the most shallow.
insights.quote: He singled out Twitter as the worst offender.
insights.locator: So much of what we do on social media
